title: Dominant representatives of affine-reflection error weights descend
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], with these terms as defined in [lem-sfb-rho-section-modules]. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq B\subseteq S$, with $B$ a Borel subgroup, and use $X=X^*(T)$, roots $\Phi$, positive roots $\Phi^+$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$, simple roots $\Delta$, coroots and their pairing from [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Let $B^-$ be the Borel opposite to $B$ relative to $T$, so its roots are $-\Phi^+$. Put $\rho=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha\in X$, $Q=\mathbf Z\Phi$, and $W=N_S(T)(F)/T(F)$, acting on $X$ by normalizer conjugation. Set $w\mathbin\cdot x=w(x+\rho)-\rho$, let $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$, and put $N=|\Phi^+|$. A rational module for any group here is an $F$-vector space with a coassociative counital coaction into its tensor product with that group's coordinate algebra; a submodule is a coaction-stable subspace. For $x\in X$, let $F_x$ be the one-dimensional $B^-$-module on which $T$ acts by $x$ and the unipotent radical acts trivially. For a finite-dimensional rational $B^-$-module $M$, let $\mathcal L(M)$ be the sheaf of sections of $S\times^{B^-}M$ on $S/B^-$: over $V\subseteq S/B^-$ its sections are regular maps $f:\pi^{-1}(V)\to M$ with $f(gb)=b^{-1}f(g)$, where $\pi:S\to S/B^-$ is the quotient. Write $H^i(M)=H^i(S/B^-,\mathcal L(M))$ for Zariski sheaf cohomology, with its natural left $S$-action, and $H^i(x)=H^i(F_x)$; set $H^i=0$ for $i<0$. Equivariance means a coaction identity, hence holds after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. A simple module is nonzero with no proper nonzero rational submodule, and a simple constituent means a simple subquotient. Set $D=\{x\in X:\langle x+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }\alpha\in\Delta\}$. Write $y\le x$ when $x-y$ is an integral nonnegative sum of simple roots, and $y<x$ when also $y\ne x$. Define $y\uparrow x$ to mean there is a finite chain $y=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_m=x$ where each step has $x_{j-1}=s_{\beta_j}\mathbin\cdot x_j+n_jp\beta_j\le x_j$ for some $\beta_j\in\Phi^+$ and integer $n_j\ge0$. Each finite dot orbit has a unique representative $d(y)\in D$, and $<$ is well founded on $D$. The finite Weyl group has the Coxeter length $\ell$ for its simple reflections, with $\ell(w_0)=N$. If $x\in D$, $\alpha\in\Delta$, $w\in W$ and $y=w\mathbin\cdot x$ satisfy $\ell(s_\alpha w)=\ell(w)+1$, then $r=\langle y+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0$. For every integer $k$ with $0<kp<r$, put $z=s_\alpha\mathbin\cdot y+kp\alpha$. Then
$$d(z)<x\qquad\text{and}\qquad d(z)\uparrow x.$$
These assertions hold for reducible and empty finite root systems and all positive primes.

source.place: Definition 1, Proposition 1 and Lemma 1, pp.54--55 (dominant-chamber reduction for strong linkage); reduced-word positive roots on p.57; Lemma 5 and its proof on p.58 (strict decrease and strong linkage for all intermediate error weights). Lemma 1 cites Jantzen 1977, Satz 9. This is root-system geometry, not representation-theoretic linkage.

proof.text:
By [lem-sfb-semisimple-roots-span], the roots span $E=X\otimes\mathbf Q$. By [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization], $W$ is finite and acts on $E$ as the root-reflection group. The simple reflections generate it by [lem-sfb-simple-root-reflection-generation]. On $V=E\otimes\mathbf R$ choose a positive definite form $b_0$ in any basis and put $b(u,v)=\sum_{a\in W}b_0(au,av)$. Reindexing gives $W$-invariance, and the identity summand makes $b$ positive definite. Since $s_\beta\beta=-\beta$, invariance and the root-datum reflection formula give
$$2b(v,\beta)=\langle v,\beta^\vee\rangle b(\beta,\beta).$$
A simple reflection permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha\}$: any other positive root has a positive coefficient at another simple root, unchanged by subtracting a multiple of $\alpha$; reducedness excludes a distinct positive root supported only at $\alpha$. Thus the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion] hold on $V$, with the simple roots and this form.

source.place: Milne Appendix C.10--C.11 and C.19--C.22; Andersen p.54, finite-root-system preliminaries.

proof.text:
For a reduced word $a=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_m}$, every root $\gamma_j=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_{j-1}}\alpha_j$ is positive. Otherwise apply [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion] to the prefix and the positive root $\alpha_j$: appending $s_{\alpha_j}$ deletes a letter, contradicting minimality of this prefix of the reduced word. The empty prefix sends $\alpha_1$ to itself. If $u\in D$ and $v=u+\rho$, telescoping the successive prefixes gives
$$v-av=\sum_{j=1}^m\langle v,\alpha_j^\vee\rangle\gamma_j.$$
Each coefficient is a nonnegative integer, and each $\gamma_j$ is an integral nonnegative sum of simple roots. Therefore $a\mathbin\cdot u\le u$. This derives the orbit bound directly; it does not cite full faithfulness or merely the definition of a chamber as a substitute for a closed-chamber theorem.

source.place: Andersen p.54, fundamental-domain observation; p.58, Lemma 5, the finite-Weyl orbit bound. Explicit reduced-word derivation from exchange.

proof.text: Every finite dot orbit has a maximal element for $\le$: the simple-root coordinates make this a partial order, and the orbit is finite by step 1. If a maximal element $u$ has $\langle u+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle<0$, then $s_\alpha\mathbin\cdot u=u-\langle u+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha>u$, a contradiction. Thus it lies in $D$. If two elements $u,v\in D$ are in the same orbit, step 2 gives both $u\le v$ and $v\le u$, hence $u=v$. This proves the asserted existence and uniqueness of $d$. Moreover, successive folds $f_\alpha$ can take any weight to its $d$: a nontrivial fold strictly increases the weight in this finite orbit, so a sequence that always folds a negative simple pairing must terminate, and its terminal weight lies in $D$.

source.place: Andersen p.54, Proposition 1 preliminary chamber representative; explicit finite-poset construction, also for singular weights.

proof.text:
The half-sum node [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit] gives $\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$ for every simple $\alpha$, so $b(\alpha,\rho)=b(\alpha,\alpha)/2>0$. For $u\in D$, the reflection identity of step 1 gives $b(u+\rho,\alpha)\ge0$ for simple roots; expanding positive roots then gives
$$b(u+\rho,\rho)=\tfrac12\sum_{\beta\in\Phi^+}b(u+\rho,\beta)\ge0.$$
Fix $x\in D$. For $u\in D$, $u\le x$, write uniquely $x-u=\sum_\alpha n_\alpha\alpha$, with integral $n_\alpha\ge0$. The preceding inequality bounds $\sum_\alpha n_\alpha b(\alpha,\rho)\le b(x+\rho,\rho)$. Each coefficient is therefore bounded, so there are only finitely many such $u$. Consequently every nonempty subset of $D$ has a $<$-minimal element: choose $x$ in it and a minimal element in its finite intersection with $\{u:u\le x\}$. Any smaller element of the subset would belong to that intersection. This proves well-foundedness.

source.place: Andersen p.57, dominance induction; explicit positive functional and finite-lower-interval justification. Milne 21.72 for rho.

proof.text: Let $\ell(s_\alpha w)=\ell(w)+1$. If $w^{-1}\alpha$ were negative, put $\beta=-w^{-1}\alpha\in\Phi^+$. Then $w\beta=-\alpha$ and [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion] applied to a reduced word for $w$ gives a word for $ws_\beta$ with $\ell(w)-1$ letters. Conjugating the orthogonal reflection formula gives $ws_\beta w^{-1}=s_{w\beta}=s_\alpha$; faithfulness from step 1 makes this an equality in $W$. Thus $s_\alpha w=ws_\beta$ contradicts the length hypothesis. Hence $w^{-1}\alpha$ is positive. Since $x\in D$, step 1 and its positive simple-root expansion give $b(x+\rho,w^{-1}\alpha)\ge0$. By invariance this is $b(y+\rho,\alpha)$; the reflection identity implies $r=\langle y+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ge0$.

source.place: Andersen p.57, positive roots of a reduced word; explicit exchange proof for the length-increasing case.

proof.text: Fix $0<kp<r$. The identity $z=y-(r-kp)\alpha$ gives one affine lowering edge, so $z\uparrow y$. Apply [lem-sfb-simple-chamber-fold-affine-step] to every edge of a chain: concatenating its at-most-two-edge replacements proves $f_\delta(u)\uparrow f_\delta(v)$ whenever $u\uparrow v$. Its lattice, root, coroot and base hypotheses are the root-datum hypotheses here, and $p>0$, $\rho\in X$. Choose the finite sequence of folds taking $y$ to $d(y)=x$ supplied in step 3. Fold both ends of the chain simultaneously at each stage. The lower endpoint becomes some $z'$ in the finite dot orbit of $z$, and $z'\uparrow x$. Now choose folds taking $z'$ to $d(z')=d(z)$. Each fold fixes $x$, since all its shifted simple pairings are nonnegative, so the same edge-replacement argument keeps the upper endpoint equal to $x$. The final chain gives $d(z)\uparrow x$. Summing its simple-root differences gives $d(z)\le x$.

source.place: Andersen Lemma 1, pp.54--55, chamber reduction, expanded by local edge rewriting; application in Lemma 5, p.58.

proof.text:
Put $v=y+\rho$ and $t=r-kp$. Both $t$ and $kp$ are strictly positive, and $z+\rho=v-t\alpha$. The reflection identity of step 1 gives
$$b(v,v)-b(z+\rho,z+\rho)=t(r-t)b(\alpha,\alpha)=(r-kp)kp\,b(\alpha,\alpha)>0.$$
If $d(z)=x$, then $z+\rho$ and $y+\rho$ would belong to the same finite $W$-orbit as $x+\rho$, and invariance of $b$ would make their squared norms equal, a contradiction. Combining this with step 6 gives $d(z)<x$. All calculations take place in the real character space, so are unaffected by the characteristic of $F$; the integer $p$ need only be positive. No irreducibility is used. For the empty root system step 1 gives $V=0$ and $W=\{1\}$, hence $D=\{0\}$, and there is no simple root or allowed error weight; the representative and well-foundedness assertions still hold.

source.place: Andersen Lemma 5, p.58, strict descent; explicit invariant squared-norm calculation, including the rank-zero case.

proof.text: Finally $\ell(w_0)=N$, where $w_0$ is the unique element with $w_0\Phi^+=-\Phi^+$ given by [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit]. For $w\in W$ put $n(w)=|\{\beta\in\Phi^+:w\beta\in-\Phi^+\}|$. Since $s_\alpha$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha\}$ and negates $\alpha$ (step 1), $n(ws_\alpha)\le n(w)+1$; induction on a word gives $n(w)\le\ell(w)$, so $N=n(w_0)\le\ell(w_0)$. Conversely let $w_0=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_m}$ be reduced, $a_k=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_k}$, and $\gamma_j=a_{j-1}\alpha_j$, positive by step 2. They are distinct: if $\gamma_i=\gamma_j$ with $i<j$, the invariance of $b$ and faithfulness from step 1 give $s_{\gamma_j}=a_{j-1}s_{\alpha_j}a_{j-1}^{-1}$ and $s_{\gamma_i}=a_{i-1}s_{\alpha_i}a_{i-1}^{-1}$ in $W$, so $$a_j=s_{\gamma_j}a_{j-1}=s_{\gamma_i}a_{j-1}=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_{i-1}}s_{\alpha_{i+1}}\cdots s_{\alpha_{j-1}}$$ has a word of $j-2$ letters, contradicting reducedness of the prefix $a_j$. Hence $m\le|\Phi^+|=N$, and $\ell(w_0)=N$. For $\Phi=\varnothing$ both sides are $0$.
